html:
Saba, the biblical Sheba, was an ancient kingdom in the southwest of Arabia, in today's Yemen. Its capital was Marib, on the edge of the desert, and its people were the Sabaeans. The map shows it from 1500 to 100 BCE, though its inscriptions begin only around 1000 BCE.

Saba grew rich on the incense trade. Frankincense and myrrh, resins from trees of South Arabia and the Horn of Africa, were burned in temples and used in medicine from Rome to Mesopotamia, and camel caravans carried them north up the west of Arabia to Gaza and Damascus. The Sabaeans taxed and guarded this trade.

Their greatest work was the Marib dam, an earth and stone dam that caught the seasonal floods of the Wadi Dhana and watered two large oases. It was repaired many times over more than a thousand years.

The Bible tells of the Queen of Sheba visiting King Solomon with gifts of gold and spices; the story cannot be checked, but it shows Saba's fame. The Sabaeans wrote in the South Arabian script, and their rulers, called mukarribs and later kings, left many inscriptions.

Saba was one of several South Arabian kingdoms, along with Qataban, Hadramaut and Ma'in, which competed for the trade. Sabaeans also settled across the Red Sea in Ethiopia and influenced the culture there that came before Aksum. In the first centuries CE the trade shifted to the sea, and the Himyarites rose to the south. They conquered Saba around 275 CE.
